mainTopic: Oaths about a מצוה and the קרבן of שבועת ביטוי; proving that 'להרע או להיטיב' refers to optional matters
overview: The משנה rules that if a person swears to refrain from a מצוה, or to do a מצוה, and then breaks the oath, he does not bring the קרבן for a שבועת ביטוי. רבי יהודה בן בתירא argues with a קל וחומר that an oath to do a מצוה should make him חייב, and the חכמים reject his argument. The גמרא brings a ברייתא that learns from 'להרע או להיטיב' that this קרבן applies only to optional (רשות) matters. So oaths about a מצוה are excluded. An oath to harm oneself counts, an oath to harm others does not, and an oath to do good for others counts. The גמרא then asks how we know the פסוק is about optional matters. A first proof from comparing 'harm' to 'good' is rejected. A second proof comes from the extra word 'או', which would be unnecessary if the פסוק were about מצוות. The גמרא asks whether 'או' is needed to separate the cases, and answers that no פסוק is needed for that. It then notes that this answer fits רבי יונתן but not רבי יאשיה, and it brings their מחלוקת about cursing a father and mother. The answer for רבי יאשיה continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה's ruling on oaths about a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that one who swears to refrain from a מצוה, or to perform a מצוה, and breaks the oath is פטור. The second case would logically be חייב according to רבי יהודה בן בתירא.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone swore not to do a מצוה and then did it, he is exempt. If he swore to do a מצוה and did not do it, he is also exempt, even though it would make sense to say he is liable, as רבי יהודה בן בתירא argues.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives two rulings: breaking an oath about a מצוה, in either direction, does not bring a קרבן. It also tells us that רבי יהודה בן בתירא disagrees with the second ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two cases. The first is swearing to refrain from a מצוה and then doing it anyway. The second is swearing to do a מצוה and then not doing it. Both are פטור. The words 'שהיה בדין' signal that a logical argument for חיוב exists in the second case, and the next step lays it out.

keyTerms.meaning: To refrain from (not do) a מצוה
Exempt, here from the קרבן of שבועת ביטוי
By logic / it would be reasonable

steps.confusionAlert: 'לבטל את המצוה' does not mean cancelling the oath. It means swearing NOT to do a מצוה. Also, 'פטור' here means he brings no קרבן for breaking the oath.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
If one swore to refrain from a מצוה
and did not refrain, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: Exempt from the קרבן a person brings for breaking a שבועת ביטוי.

phrases.english: If he swore to perform it and did not perform it, he is exempt;
though it would have been logical that he be liable,
according to the words of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִשְׁבַּע לְבַטֵּל אֶת הַמִּצְוָה וְלֹא בִּיטֵּל – פָּטוּר
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath about a מצוה, either to refrain from it or to do it, brings no קרבן when broken. רבי יהודה בן בתירא would make the 'to do' case חייב.

steps.title: רבי יהודה בן בתירא's קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירא argues: if an oath about an optional matter makes a person חייב, then an oath about a מצוה, which he already swore to keep at הר סיני, should certainly make him חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירא said: Think about it. An optional matter was never sworn about at הר סיני, yet a person is liable for breaking an oath about it. A מצוה was sworn about at הר סיני. Shouldn't he surely be liable for breaking an oath to keep it?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה בן בתירא proves his position with a קל וחומר, an 'all the more so' argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'lighter' case is a רשות matter, which carries no earlier oath, and still brings a חיוב. The 'heavier' case is a מצוה, which already carries the oath from הר סיני. So a new oath to do it should certainly bring a חיוב.

keyTerms.meaning: If even…; the opening of a קל וחומר
An optional matter, neither commanded nor forbidden
Already under oath from הר סיני
Isn't it logical…? (end of a קל וחומר)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira said:
If regarding an optional matter,
about which he is not under oath from Mount Sinai,
he is liable for breaking an oath about it;

phrases.aramaic: מִצְוָה, שֶׁהוּא מוּשְׁבָּע עָלֶיהָ מֵהַר סִינַי –
phrases.english: then a מצוה, about which he is under oath from Mount Sinai,
is it not logical that he should be liable for it?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה אִם הָרְשׁוּת, שֶׁאֵינוֹ מוּשְׁבָּע עָלָיו מֵהַר סִינַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind 'שהיה בדין שיהא חייב' from step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That swearing to do a מצוה and not doing it should make a person חייב
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from an oath about a רשות matter

steps.title: The חכמים refute the קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer that the comparison fails. For a רשות matter, a 'no' oath is treated like a 'yes' oath. For a מצוה it is not, since swearing to refrain from a מצוה brings no חיוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: No. You can say this about an oath on an optional matter, because there the Torah treats a 'no' oath the same as a 'yes' oath. But can you say it about an oath on a מצוה, where the Torah does not treat 'no' like 'yes'? After all, if someone swore not to do a מצוה and did it, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים knock down רבי יהודה בן בתירא's קל וחומר by showing that the 'lighter' case has a strength the 'heavier' case lacks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר only works if the lighter case is weaker in every relevant way. With a רשות oath, both a לאו oath and a הן oath bring a חיוב. With a מצוה, the לאו oath is פטור, as the first ruling of the משנה says. So oaths about a מצוה are a weaker category, and the קל וחומר falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: No. If you said X… (the formula for refuting a קל וחומר)

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's הלכה follows the חכמים: oaths about a מצוה bring no קרבן in either direction. Their answer only knocks down רבי יהודה בן בתירא's קל וחומר. The source for the exemption in the פסוק comes in the ברייתא (steps 5 and 7).

phrases.english: They said to him: No. If you said this
regarding an oath about an optional matter,
where the Torah made the negative like the positive,
phrases.notes: In other words, swearing 'I won't' counts just like swearing 'I will'.

phrases.english: will you say the same regarding an oath about a מצוה,
where the Torah did not make the negative like the positive;

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאִם נִשְׁבַּע לְבַטֵּל וְלֹא בִּיטֵּל – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: for if he swore to refrain and did not refrain, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: לֹא אִם אָמַרְתָּ בִּשְׁבוּעַת הָרְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the קל וחומר of step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole קל וחומר of רבי יהודה בן בתירא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The lighter case (רשות) has a strength the heavier case (מצוה) lacks: its לאו oath is treated like its הן oath.

steps.title: The ברייתא raises a possible assumption
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא suggests we might have thought that swearing to refrain from a מצוה and then doing it would make a person חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: You might think that if someone swore not to do a מצוה and then did it, he would be liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that opens with a possible mistaken assumption. This is a setup line; the ברייתא answers it with a פסוק in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה stated the first ruling (לבטל is פטור) without giving a source from a פסוק. The ברייתא now looks for a Torah source. It first states the opposite idea that someone might have held.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable, here to bring the קרבן

phrases.english: GEMARA:
The Rabbis taught:
One might think that if one swore to refrain from a מצוה
and did not refrain, he would be liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: יָכוֹל נִשְׁבַּע לְבַטֵּל אֶת הַמִּצְוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Seeks a Torah source for the first ruling of the משנה (step 1).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an oath to refrain from a מצוה, once broken, brings a קרבן

steps.title: The verse limits liability to optional matters
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns from 'להרע או להיטיב' that 'doing good' means optional actions, so 'doing harm' does too. That excludes an oath to refrain from a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'to do harm or to do good.' Just as 'doing good' is about optional things, 'doing harm' is also about optional things. So I exclude someone who swore not to do a מצוה and then did it: he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its question with a פסוק and proves that an oath to refrain from a מצוה is פטור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two halves of the פסוק are read as parallel. 'Doing good' (להיטיב) must refer to רשות matters, so 'doing harm' (להרע) must also refer to רשות matters. Refraining from a מצוה is not a רשות matter, so it falls outside the פרשה of שבועת ביטוי.

keyTerms.meaning: To do harm or to do good (ויקרא 5:4)
Just as… so too… (a parallel comparison)

steps.whatToRemember: The source for the משנה's first ruling: 'להרע או להיטיב' speaks only about optional matters, so an oath to refrain from a מצוה brings no קרבן.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic boundary of שבועת ביטוי: the קרבן applies to oaths about optional actions, not to oaths that go against the Torah's commands.

phrases.english: The verse states: "To do harm or to do good"
just as doing good refers to an optional matter,
so too, doing harm refers to an optional matter;
I will exclude one who swore to refrain from a מצוה
and did not refrain, so that he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'יכול' question of step 4 with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is פטור, because the פסוק limits שבועת ביטוי to רשות matters (להרע is parallel to להיטיב).

steps.title: What if he swore to do a מצוה and did not do it?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises a new possibility: maybe a person who swears to do a מצוה and then fails to do it is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think that if someone swore to keep a מצוה and then did not keep it, he would be חייב.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is setting up its next case. It suggests that someone who swears to do a מצוה and then fails to do it might be חייב a קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 dealt with an oath to stay away from a מצוה. Now the ברייתא flips to the opposite case: an oath to actually do a מצוה. The question is whether breaking that kind of oath makes him חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You might think': opens a suggestion the ברייתא will then reject

phrases.english: One might think: one who swore to fulfill the מצוה
and did not fulfill it, that he would be liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from an oath to refrain from a מצוה (step 5) to an oath to perform a מצוה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is one who swears to perform a מצוה and does not perform it חייב?

steps.title: An oath to do a מצוה is excluded
steps.stepSummary: From 'להרע או להיטיב': just as 'doing harm' means an optional matter, 'doing good' also means an optional matter. So an oath to do a מצוה is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'to do harm or to do good.' Just as 'doing harm' is about optional things, 'doing good' is also about optional things. So I leave out someone who swore to do a מצוה and did not do it. He is פטור.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that someone who breaks an oath to do a מצוה is פטור. The פסוק only covers oaths about optional matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two halves of the פסוק are compared to each other. 'Doing harm' is about optional matters, so 'doing good' must be too. A מצוה is not optional, so an oath about it is left out.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The פסוק teaches': introduces the source in the פסוק
an optional matter, something a person is free to choose
'I will exclude': leave this case out of the rule

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the direction of the comparison. In step 5, 'doing good' taught us about 'doing harm.' Here it is the opposite: 'doing harm' teaches us about 'doing good.' Each half of the פסוק can teach about the other.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "To do harm or to do good"

phrases.aramaic: מָה הֲרָעָה רְשׁוּת, אַף הֲטָבָה רְשׁוּת;
phrases.english: just as doing harm is optional, so too doing good is optional;
I will exclude one who swore to fulfill the מצוה
and did not fulfill it, that he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the suggestion of step 6
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is פטור, because 'להיטיב' is compared to 'להרע' and so refers only to optional matters, not to a מצוה.

steps.title: What if he swore to harm himself and did not?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests that an oath to harm oneself might not count, so breaking it would be פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think that if someone swore to harm himself and then did not harm himself, he would be פטור.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא sets up a new case: an oath to hurt yourself. Maybe, since it is a 'harmful' thing, breaking that oath does not make you חייב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the suggestion leans toward פטור, not חייב. The thought is that an oath to harm oneself is not a normal oath that the תורה would want kept.

phrases.english: One might think: one who swore to harm himself
and did not harm himself, one might think he would be exempt?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next case in the ברייתא's list
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is one who swears to harm himself and does not do it פטור?

steps.title: An oath to harm oneself is included
steps.stepSummary: Just as 'doing good' is optional, 'doing harm' is optional too. Harming himself is up to him, so he is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'to do harm or to do good.' Just as 'doing good' is about optional things, 'doing harm' is too. So I include someone who swore to harm himself and did not. He is חייב, because that choice is in his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא rules that this person is חייב. Harming himself is his own choice, so it counts as an optional matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is not whether the action is 'good' or 'bad.' The test is whether the person is free to choose it. Hurting yourself is your own decision, so the oath falls under the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Just as ... so too': a comparison between two things
'I will include': bring this case into the rule
since the choice is in his hands

steps.whyThisMatters: This step shows the real test of the whole ברייתא. An oath counts if the matter is truly up to the person, whether it sounds good or bad.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "To do harm or to do good"

phrases.aramaic: מָה הֲטָבָה רְשׁוּת, אַף הֲרָעָה רְשׁוּת;
phrases.english: just as doing good is optional, so too doing harm is optional;
I will include one who swore to harm himself
and did not harm himself, since the choice is in his hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is חייב, because harming himself is his own choice, so it counts as רשות.

steps.title: What if he swore to harm others and did not?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests that someone who swore to harm other people and did not do it might be חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think that if someone swore to harm others and then did not harm them, he would be חייב.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא sets up the next case: an oath to hurt someone else. Since an oath to hurt yourself counts, maybe this one counts too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 might make us think any oath 'to do harm' counts. So the ברייתא asks whether harming other people is also included.

phrases.english: One might think: one who swore to harm others
and did not harm them, that he would be liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the 'harm' case from oneself to others
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is one who swears to harm others and does not do it חייב?

steps.title: An oath to harm others is excluded
steps.stepSummary: Using the same comparison, 'doing harm' means only optional matters. Hurting others is not his choice to make, so he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'to do harm or to do good.' Just as 'doing good' is optional, 'doing harm' is optional too. So I leave out someone who swore to harm others and did not. That choice is not in his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא rules that this person is פטור. He has no right to hurt other people, so this is not an optional matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the same test as step 9 but gives the opposite result. Hurting yourself is your own choice. Hurting someone else is forbidden, so it is not a רשות matter and the oath is left out.

keyTerms.meaning: since the choice is not in his hands

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "To do harm or to do good"

phrases.aramaic: מָה הֲטָבָה רְשׁוּת, אַף הֲרָעָה רְשׁוּת;
phrases.english: just as doing good is optional, so too doing harm is optional;
I will exclude one who swore to harm others
and did not harm them, since the choice is not in his hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 10, using the same test as step 9
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is פטור, because harming others is not his right, so it is not רשות.

steps.title: Doing good for others is included
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks how we know that an oath to do good for others counts, and answers from the words 'או להיטיב'.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know to include doing good for others? The פסוק says 'or to do good.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks how we know an oath to help other people counts, and it answers from the פסוק 'או להיטיב'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Harming others was just excluded because it is not his choice. Doing good for others is something he is free to do, so it is included under the פסוק.

phrases.english: From where do we include doing good for others?
The verse teaches: "Or to do good."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 11: harming others is excluded, but doing good for others is included
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An oath to do good for others counts, learned from 'או להיטיב'.

steps.title: An example of harming others
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives an example of 'harming others': 'I will strike so-and-so and split open his head.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What counts as harming others? Saying, 'I will hit so-and-so and crack his skull.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains what it means by 'harming others' by giving a clear example of a violent oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The example shows the kind of harm meant in step 11: actually hurting another person's body. That is plainly forbidden, so it can never be a רשות matter.

keyTerms.meaning: and I will wound or split open

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's rule: an oath counts only for matters that are up to the person. A מצוה (to do it or to avoid it) does not count. Harming others does not count. Harming yourself counts. Doing good for others counts.

phrases.english: And what is harming others?
"I will strike so-and-so
and split open his brain."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the 'harming others' case excluded in step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Harming others means an oath like 'I will strike so-and-so and split open his head.'

steps.title: Maybe the פסוק is about מצוה matters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's starting point: how do we know the פסוקים are about optional matters? Maybe they are about מצוה matters.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know these פסוקים are talking about optional matters? Maybe they are talking about מצוה matters!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions the whole basis of the ברייתא. Every case above assumed the פסוק is about רשות, and the גמרא asks how we know that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each comparison above ('just as ... so too') started from the idea that one half of the פסוק is about optional things. The גמרא suggests both halves might instead be about מצוות, which would turn the ברייתא's rules upside down.

keyTerms.meaning: and from where do we know?

phrases.english: And from where do we know that the verses
are written about an optional matter?
Perhaps they are written about a מצוה matter!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps back and challenges the assumption behind all the ברייתא's comparisons
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's assumption that 'להרע או להיטיב' refers to רשות matters
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every 'just as ... so too' comparison depends on one half of the פסוק being about optional matters. If the פסוק is really about מצוה matters, that starting point falls away, and the ברייתא's results lose their basis.

steps.title: Harm and good must match, so doing harm can't be about מצוות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the פסוק compares הרעה to הטבה. If we read it about מצוות, 'doing harm' would turn into doing good.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that! We need doing good to be like doing harm, and doing harm to be like doing good, because the פסוק puts them side by side. If the פסוק were about מצוות, then doing good would never mean skipping a מצוה. So doing harm would also never mean skipping a מצוה. That means 'doing harm' would really be doing good!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the idea from step 14 that the פסוקים might be about מצוה matters. It uses the comparison between 'harm' and 'good' to show that this reading falls apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the פסוק pairs הרעה with הטבה, whatever is true of one must be true of the other. In a מצוה setting, 'good' means doing a מצוה, so 'harm' would also have to mean doing a מצוה. Then 'harm' is no longer harm at all, which makes no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק compared (linked) one thing to another

phrases.english: This should not enter your mind;
since we require doing good to be similar to doing harm,
and doing harm to be similar to doing good;
for the verse compares doing harm to doing good –
just as doing good does not involve skipping a מצוה,
so too doing harm does not involve skipping a מצוה.
So 'doing harm' itself is really doing good!

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ; דְּבָעֵינַן הֲטָבָה דּוּמְיָא דַּהֲרָעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 14 by showing that the מצוה reading leads to a contradiction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical contradiction from the הקש between הרעה and הטבה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוקים might be talking about מצוה matters.
steps.terutzMaskana: A מצוה reading would turn 'harm' into 'good', so the פסוקים must be about optional matters.

steps.title: The comparison also works in reverse
steps.stepSummary: Comparing הטבה to הרעה in a מצוה reading would also make 'doing good' turn into harm.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the פסוק also compares doing good to doing harm. Doing harm never means doing a מצוה, so doing good would also never mean doing a מצוה. That means 'doing good' would really be doing harm!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its argument by running the same comparison in the other direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now 'harm' sets the rule: in a מצוה setting, harm means not doing a מצוה. So 'good' would also have to mean not doing a מצוה, which is really harm. Whichever direction you compare, the מצוה reading falls apart.

phrases.english: And the verse compares doing good to doing harm –
just as doing harm does not involve fulfilling a מצוה,
so too doing good does not involve fulfilling a מצוה.
So 'doing good' itself is really doing harm!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer from step 15 by applying the comparison in the opposite direction.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A מצוה reading could still work if you only compare in one direction.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both directions break down, so a מצוה reading does not work.

steps.title: That argument would wreck optional matters too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the same twisting argument could also be used against reading the פסוקים as optional matters.
steps.simpleTranslation: If that is how you argue, then you could not apply the פסוק to optional matters either!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from steps 15-16. It says this kind of reasoning proves too much.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we force harm and good to match in every detail, we could produce the same kind of contradiction for optional matters too. Then the פסוק would fit nothing at all. So the comparison argument cannot be what proves the פסוקים are about optional matters.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is how it works
An optional matter, something not commanded or forbidden
You will not find it (any case where it applies)

phrases.english: If so,

phrases.aramaic: בִּדְבַר הָרְשׁוּת נָמֵי לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ!
phrases.english: you would not find it applying to optional matters either!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, בִּדְבַר הָרְשׁוּת נָמֵי לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof given in steps 15-16.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The argument proves too much. It would also cancel out the optional-matters reading, leaving the פסוק with no meaning.

steps.title: The extra word 'או' proves it is about optional matters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new proof: the תורה needed the word 'או' to include doing good to others. That shows the פסוקים are about optional matters.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the proof is this: the תורה needed the word 'או' to include doing good to others. Learn from this that the פסוקים are about optional matters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the comparison argument and brings a different proof, based on the extra word 'או' from step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 12 the ברייתא learned from 'או להיטיב' that an oath to do good for others counts. The fact that a special word was needed tells us something about what the פסוקים are discussing. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from this; we can conclude

phrases.english: Rather, since the word 'or' was needed
phrases.notes: This is the 'או' of 'או להיטיב' from step 12 (ויקרא 5:4).

phrases.english: to include doing good to others –
conclude from this that the verses are written about optional matters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected comparison proof with a new proof from the extra word 'או'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New proof from a word that would otherwise be extra
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The comparison between harm and good proves the פסוקים are about optional matters.
steps.terutzMaskana: The proof comes from the need for 'או' to include doing good to others.

steps.title: In a מצוה reading, 'או' would be unnecessary
steps.stepSummary: If the פסוקים were about מצוה matters, harming others would already be included, so doing good to others would obviously count. The word 'או' would be extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if you thought the פסוקים were about מצוה matters, then harming others would already be included. Then do we really need a word to include doing good to others?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the extra word 'או' proves the פסוקים are about optional matters. This completes the answer to step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a מצוה reading, even oaths about harming others would count. If harm to others counts, then good to others obviously counts too, and no special word would be needed. Since the תורה did need 'או', the פסוקים must be about optional matters. There, harming others is excluded (step 11), so including good to others needs its own word.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter connected to a מצוה
Now that (the bigger case is true), is (the smaller case) even a question?!

steps.whatToRemember: The פסוקים of 'להרע או להיטיב' are about optional matters. The proof is that the תורה needed the extra word 'או' to include doing good to others, which would be obvious in a מצוה reading.

phrases.english: For if it should enter your mind
that the verses are written about מצוה matters;
now that doing harm to others has been included,
is it necessary to include doing good to others?!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בִּדְבַר מִצְוָה כְּתִיבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the proof in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: The פסוקים of שבועת ביטוי are about optional matters.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra word 'או' would be unnecessary in a מצוה reading, because good to others would follow from harm to others.

steps.title: Maybe 'or' is needed to separate the cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the previous proof. The word 'או' may be needed to teach that each case alone makes you liable, not to include doing good to others.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this word 'or' is needed to separate the cases!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from the word 'או'. It says the word has a different job: to separate 'harm' from 'good' so that either one alone counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 19 the proof depended on 'או' being an extra word. Now the גמרא says it is not extra. Without it, the פסוק would read 'to harm and to do good,' and we might think you are only liable for an oath that covers both together. If 'או' has this job, the proof that the פסוקים are about optional matters falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: To separate, so that each item counts on its own

phrases.english: But this word 'or'
phrases.notes: This is the 'או' in 'לְהָרַע אוֹ לְהֵיטִיב', the word the last proof was built on.

phrases.english: is needed to separate!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof from steps 18-19 by giving 'או' a different job
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'או' is extra and so must include doing good to others
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'או' is needed to teach that each case alone makes you liable, it is not extra, and nothing can be learned from it about optional matters.

steps.title: No פסוק is needed to separate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we don't need a פסוק to teach separation. We would know that anyway, so 'או' is still extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: To separate, a פסוק is not needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It says splitting the cases apart is obvious and needs no extra word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the פסוק said 'to harm and to do good,' we would understand that each one alone counts. So 'או' is not doing the job of separating, and the proof from step 19 still stands.

phrases.english: To separate, a verse is not needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20
steps.terutzResolutionType: Denies that the word is needed for the other teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'או' is needed so that each case alone makes you liable
steps.terutzMaskana: Each case counts on its own even without a special word, so 'או' stays extra

steps.title: That only works for רבי יונתן; what about רבי יאשיה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the answer in step 21 only fits רבי יונתן. רבי יאשיה holds that a פסוק is needed to separate.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for רבי יונתן, but for רבי יאשיה, what can be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges its own answer. It says the idea that 'no פסוק is needed to separate' is only one opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known מחלוקת about the word 'and' in a פסוק. רבי יונתן says it automatically covers each item alone. רבי יאשיה says it only means both together unless a פסוק teaches otherwise. For רבי יאשיה, 'או' would be needed to separate, so the proof from 'או' seems to fail.

keyTerms.meaning: What can be said? (How will you answer?)

phrases.english: This works well according to Rabbi Yonatan,
but according to Rabbi Yoshiya,
what can be said?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן, אֶלָּא לְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the answer of step 21 only works for one תנא
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that 'no פסוק is needed to separate'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יאשיה does need a פסוק to separate, so for him 'או' has a job and is not extra.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two names. רבי יונתן is the one who says 'and' already includes each one alone. רבי יאשיה is the one who needs a פסוק for that.

steps.title: The ברייתא: רבי יאשיה on cursing father and mother
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show רבי יאשיה's view. He needs a special reading of the פסוק to teach that cursing just a father or just a mother makes you liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'A man who curses his father and his mother.' From this I only know about his father and mother together. How do I know about his father without his mother, or his mother without his father? The פסוק says: 'His father and his mother he cursed.' He cursed his father; he cursed his mother. This is the view of רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for the מחלוקת mentioned in step 22. This ברייתא shows that רבי יאשיה needs a פסוק to separate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יאשיה, 'his father and his mother' on its own means only both together. So he needs the second half of the פסוק, 'אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ קִלֵּל,' to teach that cursing either one alone counts. This proves that for him, separating needs a source in the פסוק.

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'A man who curses'
his father and his mother'
I only know about his father and his mother together;
his father but not his mother,
his mother but not his father, from where do we know?
The verse says: 'His father and his mother he cursed'
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק. He reads it as saying 'cursed' about each parent separately.

phrases.english: He cursed his father; he cursed his mother.
These are the words of Rabbi Yoshiya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the מחלוקת mentioned in step 22
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יאשיה needs a פסוק to teach that each item alone counts
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on ויקרא 20:9 about cursing a father and mother
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is the classic source for how 'and' works in a פסוק, and it shows why the proof from 'או' is in trouble for רבי יאשיה.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: 'and' means both together and each alone
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן argues. He holds that 'his father and his mother' already means both together and also each one alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן says: It means both of them together, and it means each one by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives רבי יונתן's side. He says no extra derivation is needed, because the plain wording already includes each parent alone. The statement continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יונתן, the word 'and' covers two things at once: both items together, and each item on its own. That is why, for him, 'separating' never needs a special word, which fits the answer in step 21.

keyTerms.meaning: It means; it can be understood as

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan says:
It means both of them together
and it means each one by itself,

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן אוֹמֵר: מַשְׁמָע שְׁנֵיהֶם כְּאֶחָד וּמַשְׁמָע אֶחָד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view inside the same ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word 'and' in a פסוק includes both items together and each item alone, without needing a special derivation.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יאשיה: 'and' means both together unless a פסוק teaches otherwise. רבי יונתן: 'and' means both together and each alone. The answer 'no פסוק is needed to separate' only works for רבי יונתן, so the גמרא still owes an answer for רבי יאשיה.
